Question 9
?

Given that the function f(x)=x4+2x2−x has a critical point in the interval [0,1], use the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting from x0=0.5 to estimate the critical point. Round your final answer to two decimal places.

a
x≈0.27
b
x≈0.24
c
x≈0.29
d
x≈0.20
e
x≈0.21
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

xn+1=xn−f′(xn)f″(xn),

where f′(xn) and f″(xn) are the first and second derivatives of f(x) evaluated at xn, respectively.

In our case, we have

f′(x)=(x4+2x2−x)′=4x3+4x−1,f″(x)=(4x3+4x−1)′=12x2+4.

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

xn+1=xn−4xn3+4xn−112xn2+4=xn(12xn2+4)−(4xn3+4xn−1)12xn2+4=8xn3+112xn2+4.

Starting with x0=0.5, we have

x1=8x03+112x02+4=8(0.5)3+112(0.5)2+4=0.285714….

Similarly, we have

x2=8x13+112x12+4=8(0.285714…)3+112(0.285714…)2+4=0.238290…,x3=8x23+112x22+4=8(0.238290…)3+112(0.238290…)2+4=0.236734….

Notice that the last two approximations x2≈0.24 and x3≈0.24 are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is x≈0.24, rounded to two decimal places.
name: Question 9
problem: Given that the function $f(x)={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}-x$ has a critical point in the interval $[0,1],$ use the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting from ${x}_{0}=0.5$ to estimate the critical point. Round your final answer to two decimal places.
worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}-x)^{′}=4{x}^{3}+4x-1, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(4{x}^{3}+4x-1)^{′}=12{x}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{4{x}_{n}^{3}+4{x}_{n}-1}{12{x}_{n}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}(12{x}_{n}^{2}+4)-(4{x}_{n}^{3}+4{x}_{n}-1)}{12{x}_{n}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8{x}_{n}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{n}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=0.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{8{x}_{0}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{0}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8(0.5)^{3}+1}{12(0.5)^{2}+4} \\  & =0.285\,714….\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{8{x}_{1}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{1}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8(0.285\,714…)^{3}+1}{12(0.285\,714…)^{2}+4} \\  & =0.238\,290…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{8{x}_{2}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{2}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8(0.238\,290…)^{3}+1}{12(0.238\,290…)^{2}+4} \\  & =0.236\,734….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{2}≈0.24$ and ${x}_{3}≈0.24$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈0.24,$ rounded to two decimal places.
